dip-buying.definition: Buying an asset right after its price has dropped sharply, on the bet that the drop was overdone and the price will recover.
dip-buying.why: Monday's rally was largely dip-buying in chip stocks after a four-week slide. It tells you investors haven't abandoned the AI story — they saw last week's prices as a discount, not a warning.
chain: Chip stocks fell hard last week on fears that AI spending would slow after the midterms.
Lower prices made those companies look cheaper relative to the earnings investors still expect.
Over the weekend no new bad news hit the sector (Nvidia's issue was company-specific), so buyers stepped back in.
Traders who had bet against the stocks rushed to close those bets, adding fuel to the bounce.
Whether the bounce lasts depends on whether the original fear — slower AI investment — is actually disproven.

relief-rally.definition: A short, sharp rise in prices during a broader downtrend, usually after selling exhausts itself or a feared event turns out less bad than expected.
relief-rally.why: The key question after a +2–3% day following four down weeks: is this a real turn or just a relief rally? Analysts look at whether gains hold through the next big catalyst — here, Tuesday's {{cpi|CPI}} report.
chain: After a long decline, many sellers have already sold — there's less selling pressure left.
Any neutral or slightly good news can then trigger outsized gains.
But if the underlying problem (here, AI-spending worries plus rising rates) hasn't changed, prices can resume falling.
A durable turn usually needs a fundamental change: better earnings, softer inflation, or a shift in Fed expectations.

magnificent-7.definition: Nickname for the seven mega-cap tech stocks — Apple, Microsoft, Alphabet, Amazon, Meta, Nvidia and Tesla — that dominate U.S. index returns.
magnificent-7.why: Together they make up roughly a third of the S&P 500's value, so how they trade largely decides whether the index is up or down. Nvidia being the only one down Monday was notable.
chain: The S&P 500 is {{cap-weighting|cap-weighted}}: bigger companies count more.
The Mag 7 grew so large that their moves now swamp the other ~490 stocks.
So a 'market' rally or sell-off is often really a Mag 7 story.
Analysts check 'breadth' (how many stocks are rising) to see whether a move is broad or concentrated.

semiconductor-etf.definition: An exchange-traded fund that holds a basket of chip-company stocks and trades like a single stock. SOXX and SMH are the best-known examples.
semiconductor-etf.why: Its daily move is a quick read on sentiment toward the whole chip sector. SOXX rising 7.5% while Nvidia — one of its biggest holdings — fell 5% shows money moved within the sector, not out of it.
chain: An ETF lets investors buy an entire sector in one trade.
Its price reflects the weighted performance of its holdings.
When one big holding falls but the ETF rises sharply, the other holdings must have risen even more.
That gap is evidence of {{sector-rotation|rotation within the sector}}.

sector-rotation.definition: Investors moving money from one group of stocks to another — between sectors, or between companies within a sector — rather than leaving the market altogether.
sector-rotation.why: Monday's chip trade was a textbook case: investors sold Nvidia on leadership risk and bought AMD, Broadcom and Marvell. Their conviction in chips didn't change; their preferred way to own it did.
chain: Weekend reports created uncertainty about Nvidia's CEO — a company-specific risk.
Investors still wanted exposure to the AI chip theme.
So they sold Nvidia and bought its peers instead.
Result: the sector ETF rose ~7.5% while its largest member fell ~5%.
Lesson: a falling leader doesn't always mean a falling theme — check what its peers are doing.

idiosyncratic-risk.definition: Risk specific to a single company — a scandal, lawsuit or failed product — as opposed to systematic risk, which hits the whole market (like interest rates or recessions).
idiosyncratic-risk.why: The investigation into Nvidia's CEO is idiosyncratic: it hurts Nvidia but not the chip industry's prospects. That's why the stock fell while peers rallied.
chain: Systematic risk (rates, the economy) moves everything together and can't be diversified away.
Idiosyncratic risk affects one name and can be diversified away by holding many stocks.
When a company-specific shock hits, investors often swap into similar companies to keep their theme exposure.
This is why diversified portfolios and ETFs dampen single-stock blowups.

cap-weighting.definition: An index method where each company's weight equals its market capitalization (share price × shares outstanding). Bigger companies move the index more.
cap-weighting.why: Over the past month the average Russell 1000 stock rose ~0.8%, yet the index lost ~$4.8 trillion in value — Nvidia alone accounted for ~$1.27 trillion of that. In a cap-weighted index, a few giants can outweigh hundreds of small winners.
chain: Market cap = price × shares; Nvidia is one of the largest companies in the world.
In a cap-weighted index, a 10% drop in Nvidia matters far more than a 10% rise in a small company.
So 'the average stock' and 'the index' can tell opposite stories.
Equal-weight indexes (every stock counts the same) are a common comparison to see the difference.

analyst-upgrade.definition: When a sell-side research analyst raises their rating on a stock (e.g., from 'Perform' to 'Outperform'), signaling they expect it to do better.
analyst-upgrade.why: Oppenheimer's upgrade of AMD, plus news that Google Cloud picked AMD chips, helped send the stock up 13% — upgrades can move prices because many investors follow these calls.
chain: Sell-side analysts at banks publish ratings and price targets for clients.
An upgrade signals new conviction, often based on a fresh catalyst (here, the Google Cloud win).
Fund managers who trust that analyst may buy, pushing the price up.
The effect is strongest when the upgrade comes alongside real business news, as it did here.

treasury-yield.definition: The annual return an investor earns for lending to the U.S. government by buying a Treasury bond. Yields move opposite to bond prices.
treasury-yield.why: Treasury yields are the base rate for almost all borrowing in the economy. The 10-year yield at 4.88% feeds directly into {{mortgage-rate|mortgage rates}} and corporate borrowing costs.
chain: A bond pays a fixed coupon; if its price falls, that fixed coupon is a bigger percentage of the price — the yield rises.
Investors demand higher yields when they expect higher inflation or higher Fed rates.
Banks and companies price their loans as a spread above Treasury yields.
So rising Treasury yields ripple out to mortgages, car loans and corporate bonds.

two-year-yield.definition: The yield on two-year U.S. government debt. Because it covers only the next couple of years, it closely tracks where traders expect the Fed's policy rate to go.
two-year-yield.why: It rose 5 {{basis-point|bp}} to 4.56% Monday — the bond market's way of saying it expects the Fed to raise rates, not cut them, in December.
chain: If you can earn the Fed's rate by rolling short-term bills, a 2-year note must offer about the average expected Fed rate over two years.
When traders expect a {{rate-hike|hike}}, that average goes up — and so does the 2-year yield.
That's why analysts call it 'the note that tracks Fed policy most closely.'
Comparing the 2-year to the 10-year (the 'yield curve') shows how the market sees short- vs. long-run rates.

basis-point.definition: One hundredth of a percentage point: 1 bp = 0.01%. A move from 4.51% to 4.56% is +5 bp.
basis-point.why: Rates people quote everything in basis points because small moves matter: on a $1 trillion of debt, 5 bp is $500 million a year in interest.
chain: Saying 'up 0.05%' is ambiguous — is that 0.05 percentage points or 5% of the rate?
Basis points remove the ambiguity: always 0.01 percentage points.
Fed moves are typically 25 bp (a quarter point).
Credit spreads, yield moves and fees are all quoted this way.

rate-hike.definition: When the Federal Reserve raises its target for the federal funds rate — the rate banks charge each other overnight — usually by 25 {{basis-point|bp}}.
rate-hike.why: The Fed hiked in September (its first in three years), held in October, and markets now see ~85% odds of another hike on Dec. 9. Higher rates cool the economy but hit stock valuations and borrowers.
chain: Inflation is running well above the Fed's 2% goal, partly from war-driven fuel prices.
The job market is strong (+165k jobs in October), so the Fed has little reason to worry about growth.
Raising rates makes borrowing more expensive, slowing spending and, eventually, inflation.
Higher rates also lower the present value of future profits — which hits long-duration growth stocks like tech hardest.

fomc.definition: The Federal Open Market Committee — the 12-member Fed committee that votes on interest rates. It meets eight times a year; the next meeting is Dec. 9.
fomc.why: Every FOMC meeting is a scheduled market event. The statement and the Chair's press conference (currently Kevin Warsh) are parsed word-by-word for hints about future moves.
chain: The FOMC includes the 7 Fed governors, the New York Fed president, and 4 rotating regional presidents.
It sets a target range for the federal funds rate.
Markets price expected decisions in advance via {{fedwatch|fed funds futures}}.
Surprises versus those expectations — not the decision itself — are what move markets.

fedwatch.definition: Fed funds futures are contracts whose payoff depends on the average fed funds rate in a given month. CME's FedWatch tool converts their prices into probabilities for each Fed meeting.
fedwatch.why: When you read '85% odds of a December hike,' this is where it comes from. It's the market's real-money bet, and it shifted sharply after Friday's jobs report.
chain: A futures price implies an expected average rate for the month.
Compare that to today's rate and you can back out how likely a move is.
Strong data (like the jobs beat) pushed the implied rate — and hike odds — higher.
Watch how these odds move after Tuesday's CPI; a big swing means the data surprised.

jobs-report.definition: The monthly Bureau of Labor Statistics release showing how many jobs the U.S. economy added (nonfarm payrolls) and the unemployment rate. Usually out the first Friday of the month.
jobs-report.why: October's report showed +165k jobs vs. much lower expectations, and unemployment fell to 4.1%. A strong labor market gives the Fed room to {{rate-hike|hike}} without fearing a recession.
chain: The Fed has a dual mandate: maximum employment and stable prices.
If employment is strong, the Fed can focus fully on fighting inflation.
A jobs 'beat' therefore raises the odds of tighter policy.
That's why the 10-year yield jumped after the report and hike odds rose to ~77–85%.

cpi.definition: A monthly measure of the average change in prices paid by consumers for a basket of goods and services, published by the BLS. The headline inflation number most people hear.
cpi.why: October CPI comes out Tuesday at 8:30 AM ET. Economists expect 3.9% year-over-year (up from 3.7%). A hot print would all but lock in a December {{rate-hike|hike}}.
chain: CPI is reported month-over-month (m/m) and year-over-year (y/y).
Markets react to the surprise versus consensus forecasts, not the level itself.
Hotter-than-expected CPI → higher expected Fed rates → higher yields → pressure on stocks.
Cooler-than-expected CPI → the opposite, often sparking rallies in rate-sensitive stocks.

core-inflation.definition: Inflation excluding food and energy prices, which swing a lot. It gives a cleaner read on underlying price pressure.
core-inflation.why: Core CPI is expected at 2.7% y/y vs. 3.9% headline — the gap is mostly war-driven fuel prices. New Fed research says oil now passes into core more than it used to, weakening the case for 'looking through' energy shocks.
chain: Central banks usually ignore one-off energy spikes because they fade on their own.
But if high oil prices raise transport and production costs, they bleed into core prices too.
Fed researchers find that pass-through has gotten stronger since the pandemic.
If true, the Fed can't simply wait out the oil shock — another reason markets expect a hike.

wti.definition: West Texas Intermediate — the main U.S. benchmark price for crude oil, traded as futures in dollars per barrel.
wti.why: WTI fell ~4.3% to ~$86.90, near its lowest since late August, on hopes the Iran war de-escalates. Cheaper oil eases inflation pressure, which could soften the case for Fed hikes.
chain: War in a major oil region raises the risk of supply disruption, pushing prices up.
Hopes for de-escalation reduce that 'risk premium,' so prices fall.
Lower oil feeds into lower gasoline (now ~$4.00 vs. $4.40 in early October).
Lower fuel prices pull down headline {{cpi|CPI}} — and, with a lag, {{core-inflation|core}}.

mortgage-rate.definition: The interest rate on a home loan. The 30-year fixed rate tracks the 10-year {{treasury-yield|Treasury yield}} plus a spread.
mortgage-rate.why: 30-year mortgage rates are around 7.2%. With the 10-year at 4.88%, housing affordability stays tight — one reason housing and regional banks feel rate moves first.
chain: Most mortgages are packaged into bonds that compete with Treasuries for investors.
So mortgage rates move with the 10-year yield, plus a spread for prepayment and credit risk.
Higher rates raise monthly payments, cooling home demand.
That slows housing activity — one channel through which Fed hikes cool the economy.

going-concern.definition: A formal disclosure that there is 'substantial doubt' a company can keep operating over the next 12 months — usually because it may run out of cash to pay its bills.
going-concern.why: Sable Offshore's stock fell 75% after its quarterly filing included going-concern language; its only crude buyer had stopped purchasing. For credit analysts, this is a red flag for default.
chain: Auditors and management must assess whether the company can meet obligations for the next year.
Relying on a single customer is concentration risk; when that buyer stopped, revenue dried up.
Without revenue, cash burns and debt payments loom.
The warning signals possible restructuring or {{chapter-11|bankruptcy}}, and equity holders are last in line.

chapter-11.definition: A form of U.S. bankruptcy that lets a company keep operating while it restructures its debts under court supervision.
chapter-11.why: JetBlue denied it plans to file for Chapter 11. A filing typically wipes out most of the value for stockholders, so even a rumor can move the stock sharply.
chain: A company that can't pay its debts can file to get court protection from creditors.
It negotiates a plan to cut or swap its debt, often converting bonds into new equity.
Creditors are paid in order of seniority; existing shareholders usually get little or nothing.
That's why going-concern warnings and bankruptcy rumors crush stock prices.

tokenization.definition: Representing ownership of a real asset — like a share of stock — as a digital token on a blockchain, so it can be traded and settled electronically.
tokenization.why: NYSE said it will use the Avalanche blockchain to settle tokenized stock trades on its planned 24/7 platform — a sign traditional exchanges are adopting blockchain rails.
chain: Today, stock trades settle one business day after the trade (T+1) through clearing houses.
A blockchain can record ownership transfer almost instantly, any hour.
That enables trading around the clock, including weekends.
Open questions: regulation, investor protection and how it links to existing systems.
